lede: Chalk in acid fizzes faster when it is powdered, faster again when the acid is warm. Both changes work the same way: they arrange more collisions between particles, or harder ones. One idea explains every way of speeding a reaction up.
can: Explain temperature, concentration and surface area through successful collisions (Higher).
Define a catalyst and name manganese(IV) oxide as the one for hydrogen peroxide.
Draw and read a reaction profile with and without a catalyst (Higher).

text: Collision theory: why a reaction speeds up

md: A reaction only happens when particles crash into each other hard enough. Everything that makes a reaction faster does it by arranging more of those crashes, or harder ones. Four changes do that, and one sentence explains all four.

prompt: Read box A in the picture above. How many of its 20 collisions a second are successful?
explain: 2 of 20. Most collisions bounce apart again, which is the whole idea this topic is built on.

md: Particles are always moving and always bumping into each other. If every bump made a reaction, everything would react at once. It does not, because a collision only works if the particles hit with at least a certain amount of energy — the **activation energy**, the **minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur**. A collision with that much energy or more is a **successful collision**.

alt: An energy-against-progress graph for an exothermic reaction: the reactant level, a hump, and a lower product level, with the height of the hump marked as the activation energy and the drop between the levels marked as the energy change.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="cpr"><title id="cpr">An exothermic reaction profile: energy against progress of reaction, with a hump between the reactant level and the product level</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><path d="M70 330 H660"/><path d="M70 330 V80"/></g><path d="M96 150 H192 C246 150 252 72 368 72 C484 72 490 268 544 268 H640" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.2"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.1" stroke-dasharray="4 4"><path d="M96 150 H498"/><path d="M640 268 H498"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3"><path d="M278 150 V78"/><path d="M274 84 l4 -6 l4 6"/><path d="M488 150 V268"/><path d="M484 262 l4 6 l4 -6"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><text x="168" y="106">activation energy</text><text x="480" y="213" text-anchor="end">energy change</text></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="76" y="140">reactants</text><text x="574" y="258">products</text><text x="368" y="368" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="500">Progress of reaction</text><text transform="translate(40 210) rotate(-90)" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="500">Energy</text><text x="70" y="52" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Reaction profile</text></g></svg>
caption: The hump is the activation energy: the energy a collision must supply before anything happens.

title: Why it is a hill and not a step
md: Before new bonds can form, bonds in the reactants have to be pulled apart, and that takes energy in. The climb is the hill. Only once the new bonds form does the energy come back down, which is why the profile rises before it falls.

prompt: On the reaction profile above, the height of the hump is the ______ energy: the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.
explain: Activation energy. It is a threshold the particles must reach on the way in, not energy the reaction gives out.

text: 2. More often: concentration and surface area (Higher)

md: Put **more particles in the same space** — a more concentrated solution — and they meet more often. Box B shows it: the collisions a second rise from 20 to 40, and the successful ones rise with them, from 2 to 4. Break a solid into smaller pieces and the same thing happens at its surface: more of the solid is exposed, so the acid meets it more often. The examiner's phrase for both is **more frequent collisions**.

prompt: In the cube picture above, the cube of side 2 cm has a surface area of 24 cm². What is the total surface area, in cm², of the 8 small cubes it is cut into?
explain: 48 cm². Each cut exposes two new faces, so the area doubles while the volume stays at 8 cm³ — the surface area to volume ratio goes from 3 to 6 cm⁻¹.

md: Raise the temperature and the particles **move faster**, which does **two** things. They meet more often, and a **greater proportion of the collisions have energy at or above the activation energy**. Box C shows both: 20 collisions a second becomes 40, and the successful ones go from 2 to 8 — a bigger jump than the collisions alone. That second idea is why a temperature answer is worth more marks than a concentration answer.

title: One thing in the video below CCEA does not examine
md: It is made for other boards and includes the **pressure of a reacting gas** as a fifth factor. CCEA's Double Award specification lists temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts only, so you never need a pressure answer here.

title: GCSE Chemistry - Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction & Collision Theory
why: A second run through the four factors, with the particle pictures animated.

prompt: Comparing box A with box C in the picture at the top of this lesson, what has raising the temperature changed?
options: both how often the particles collide and the share of collisions that succeed
only how often the particles collide
only the share of collisions that succeed
answer: both how often the particles collide and the share of collisions that succeed
explain: Both. Concentration and surface area change only the first; temperature changes both, and the mark scheme wants both ideas.

md:
**The question.** A reaction is repeated at a lower temperature. State the effect on the rate, and explain it in terms of particles. **[3]**
**Step 1 — the effect, in one clause.** The rate of reaction decreases. That is a mark on its own, so write it before any explaining.
**Step 2 — what the particles do.** They have **less energy** and move more slowly.

prompt: Which of these is the third line of that three-mark answer about lowering the temperature?
options: so there are fewer successful collisions per unit time
so the particles have less energy
answer: so there are fewer successful collisions per unit time
explain: The adjective and the time unit are the mark. 'Less collisions' earned nothing in Summer 2025, and 'less energy' is the line you have already written.

md:
**Step 3 — the collisions.** Fewer of them reach the activation energy, so there are **fewer successful collisions per unit time**. Write *successful*, and write *per unit time*: both were named by the examiners as the difference between a mark and nothing.
**The finished answer.** The rate decreases. The particles have less energy, so fewer collisions have energy at or above the activation energy, and there are fewer successful collisions per second.

title: The sentence that carries the mark
md: Summer 2025's C2 Higher report is blunt about this one. The explanation had to name **particles with less energy** and **fewer successful collisions**; *less collisions* on its own earned **nothing**, and from the next series **per unit time** is expected as well.

prompt: Complete the phrase the mark scheme wants for a raised temperature: more ______ collisions per unit time.
explain: Successful. It is one word, it is the whole mark, and it is the word most answers leave out.

md: A **catalyst** is a substance that **increases the rate of a reaction without being used up**. It is there at the end, chemically unchanged and with the same mass, and it does not appear in the equation. **Transition metals and their compounds** are often catalysts, and the one to remember by name is **manganese(IV) oxide**, $\ce{MnO2}$, for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

prompt: Name the transition metal compound used as the catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
answer: manganese(IV) oxide | manganese oxide | manganese dioxide | MnO2 | MnO₂
explain: Manganese(IV) oxide. Summer 2025's examiners were surprised how many could not name it, and it has been asked in several series.

md: A catalyst **provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy**. Look at box D: the collisions a second are unchanged at 20, but the successful ones rise from 2 to 8, because the bar the particles have to clear is lower. On the profile the dashed route starts at the same reactant level and finishes at the same product level as the solid one, so the **energy change is not altered** — only the hill between them.

prompt: On the profile above, what is different about the dashed catalysed route?
options: its hump is lower, and it starts and finishes at the same levels
it starts at a higher level, so less energy is needed
it finishes at a lower level, so more energy is given out
answer: its hump is lower, and it starts and finishes at the same levels
explain: Only the hump. Moving either end would change the energy change, and a catalyst never does that.

md: Speeding a reaction up changes **when** the product arrives, not **how much** of it there is. Add a catalyst, warm the flask or use powder and the curve is steeper and finishes sooner, but it levels off at the **same** volume, because the amounts of reactant have not changed. A question that asks why the total volume of gas is unchanged is asking for exactly that.

prompt: Looking at the three curves above: the same reaction is run again with a catalyst. What happens to the total volume of gas collected?
explain: Unchanged. The catalyst alters the speed, not the amounts of reactant, so the same product is made in less time.

md:
say that a reaction needs a collision with at least the **activation energy**, the minimum energy for a reaction to occur.
explain concentration and surface area as **more frequent collisions**.
explain temperature with **both** ideas: more frequent collisions, and more collisions with energy at or above the activation energy.
write **more (or fewer) successful collisions per unit time**, never *more collisions* on its own.
define a catalyst, name **manganese(IV) oxide**, and explain it as an **alternative pathway of lower activation energy**.

This is Question 7 of C2. The first mark is the effect in one clause — the rate increases or decreases. The last is the collision sentence, and it must carry **successful** and **per unit time**.
